prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "CISCO SYSTEMS, INC." (ticker CSCO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "CSCO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Cisco Systems, Inc.
markets: Enterprise and campus networking (switches, routers, Wi-Fi)
Data center and AI infrastructure networking for hyperscalers

mission.statement: Powering an inclusive future for all.
mission.source: Cisco company website and annual reports (stated as Cisco's purpose)
mission.plain: Cisco wants its technology to connect everyone so that everybody can benefit from the digital world.

about.plain: Cisco makes the boxes and software that move internet traffic around. Its switches, routers and Wi-Fi gear connect computers inside offices, schools, hospitals and huge data centers. It also sells security software that keeps hackers out and tools like Webex for video calls. Most of what you do online passes through Cisco equipment somewhere along the way.
about.customers: Businesses, governments, schools, telecom companies and big cloud and AI companies buy its equipment and software subscriptions.
about.everyday: When you join office Wi-Fi or a Webex video call, there is a good chance Cisco gear is carrying the data.

money.plain: switches, routers, Wi-Fi and data center networking gear
firewalls, Splunk threat detection and secure access software
Webex video meetings, calling and contact centers
Silicon One chips, high-speed switches and optics for AI data centers (about $4B of FY2026 revenue, inside Networking)
Splunk and ThousandEyes software that watches apps and networks for problems

result.summary: Cisco has a durable but no longer dominant advantage: its huge installed base, IOS/Catalyst/Meraki management tools, certified-engineer ecosystem and sales channels make it costly for enterprises to switch, and it still leads Ethernet switching (27.6% IDC share in 4Q25) and routing (30.6%). However, share has eroded to Arista, Huawei and NVIDIA in data centers, and its moat is strongest in campus and enterprise networks rather than in the fast-growing AI cloud segment, where it is now gaining ($9.3B of hyperscaler AI orders in FY2026).

pricingPower.evidence: Cisco holds a roughly 64-65% GAAP gross margin (64.5% in FY2026 vs 64.0% in FY2021) and pushed through list price increases during the 2021-2022 supply shortage while revenue still grew, but hyperscale AI customers buy at lower margins and Arista, Huawei and white-box vendors cap pricing in data centers.

moats.evidence: Cisco is the best-known enterprise networking brand and its CCNA/CCNP/CCIE certifications are the industry standard, which makes it the 'safe choice' for IT buyers; it holds a large patent portfolio.

Enterprises run decades of Cisco IOS configurations, management software (Catalyst Center, Meraki dashboard), trained staff and support contracts; services revenue of $15.0B and $46.7B of remaining performance obligations at July 2026 show how sticky the base is.
There are few direct network effects, though the large pool of Cisco-certified engineers and partners reinforces adoption indirectly.
With $63.3B of FY2026 revenue it is far larger than Arista ($9.0B in 2025) and can spread R&D, its own Silicon One chips and a global sales and support network over a vast base.
Networking markets are large and contested by Arista, HPE-Juniper, Huawei and NVIDIA, so there is no natural limit on competitors.
Cisco is the incumbent; newer rivals (Arista's single-OS model, cloud-managed and white-box networking) have counter-positioned against it rather than the reverse.
Decades of routing and switching engineering, its own Silicon One ASICs and optics (Acacia) and global support operations are hard to replicate quickly.
It owns valuable assets like Splunk's security data platform and Talos threat intelligence, but none are truly exclusive inputs rivals cannot match.

customers.evidence: Cisco's installed base spans most large enterprises and governments; services revenue held at $15.0B in FY2026 and remaining performance obligations rose 7% to $46.7B, showing high renewal and repeat purchase.

talent.evidence: Cisco ranked No. 3 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For in 2026 and has topped Great Place to Work's US and World's Best Workplaces lists in several recent years.

product.evidence: Cisco offers the broadest portfolio (campus, data center, routing, security, observability) and its Silicon One chips won hyperscaler AI business, but Arista is often rated ahead in cloud data center switching and Palo Alto and Fortinet lead in firewalls.

competitors.name: Arista Networks
competitors.note: Data center and cloud/AI switching, increasingly campus networking; 12.6% of Ethernet switching in 4Q25

competitors.name: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (incl. Juniper Networks)
competitors.note: Aruba campus/Wi-Fi, Juniper routing, Mist AI networking and data center switching

competitors.name: Huawei Technologies
competitors.note: Switches and routers, especially in China and emerging markets; 30.2% of routers and 10.6% of switching in 4Q25

competitors.name: NVIDIA
competitors.note: Spectrum-X Ethernet and InfiniBand networking for AI data centers

competitors.name: Palo Alto Networks
competitors.note: Firewalls, SASE and security operations platforms

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Teams competes with Webex; Sentinel competes with Splunk in security analytics

competitors.name: Zoom Communications
competitors.note: Video meetings, phone and contact center vs Webex

competitors.name: Datadog
competitors.note: Observability and log management vs Splunk and AppDynamics

competitors.name: Zscaler
competitors.note: Cloud security / secure access service edge

competitors.name: Nokia
competitors.note: Service provider IP routing and optical (incl. Infinera)

competitors.name: CrowdStrike
competitors.note: Security operations and next-gen SIEM vs Splunk

competitors.name: H3C Technologies
competitors.note: Switches and routers in China (majority-owned by Unisplendour)

threats: Arista and NVIDIA (Spectrum-X) winning AI and cloud data center networking, where most market growth is
Hyperscalers using white-box switches and their own designs, plus lower-margin AI deals diluting gross margin
HPE's 2025 acquisition of Juniper creating a stronger No. 2 in campus and Wi-Fi networking
Security platform leaders (Palo Alto, Fortinet, CrowdStrike, Zscaler) out-innovating Cisco's security portfolio
Webex losing ground to Microsoft Teams and Zoom; collaboration revenue is flat
Huawei dominance in China and emerging markets and geopolitical/tariff disruption to supply chains
Debt of $29.5B (after the $28B Splunk purchase) exceeding cash and investments of $15.9B

ceo.name: Chuck Robbins
ceo.background: BS in mathematics from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; joined Cisco in 1997 in sales and rose to head worldwide field operations before becoming CEO; chair since 2017

c1.evidence: Cisco leads mature enterprise networking (27.6% of Ethernet switching and 30.6% of routers in 4Q25 per IDC) and is a growing AI networking supplier with $9.3B of hyperscaler AI orders in FY2026, but it is not the leader of AI data center networking, where NVIDIA and Arista lead.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Cisco for its breadth, reliability, certified-engineer ecosystem and integrated management/support, an installed-base advantage that is durable in enterprises but has proved copyable in cloud data centers by Arista.

c3.evidence: Cisco is the default name in corporate networking among IT professionals, but most ordinary consumers do not recognise it or use its products directly.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Powering an inclusive future for all' is repeated in reports and backed by programs like Cisco Networking Academy, but management is judged mainly on revenue, margins and buybacks.

c6.evidence: “reliable, enterprise, legacy” - the impression is mostly positive among IT buyers (trusted, solid) but Cisco is often seen as an older, expensive incumbent rather than an innovator.

c7.evidence: AI data centers, cybersecurity and observability are large, growing markets (Ethernet switching alone grew 31.5% to $55.1B in 2025 per IDC), and Cisco guides FY2027 revenue to $72.2-73.4B, up about 14-16%.

c8.evidence: It has expanded into AI infrastructure (Silicon One, optics), security and observability via the $28B Splunk deal, and is researching quantum networking, but these are adjacencies of networking rather than wholly new markets.

m1.evidence: Robbins articulated the shift to software subscriptions and AI-era secure networking and executed the Splunk deal, but he is seen as a steady strategist rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Robbins is a professional manager who joined Cisco in 1997 as a sales executive; he did not found the company.

m4.evidence: Under Robbins Cisco has consistently ranked among Fortune's best workplaces (No. 3 in 2026), with a strong emphasis on employee wellbeing and customer success.

m5.evidence: He has built a highly rated, inclusive culture, but Cisco has relied heavily on acquisitions (Splunk, Acacia, ThousandEyes, Isovalent) for new technology.

m6.evidence: Robbins has a mathematics degree and a sales background rather than an engineering or product career.

m7.evidence: Robbins is known for championing social causes (Cisco's commitments to ending homelessness in Silicon Valley, racial equity programs, Networking Academy) and speaks often about technology's responsibility to society.

m7b.evidence: He gave the graduate commencement address at High Point University on April 30, 2026 (receiving an honorary doctorate), but no address at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Robbins is an affable, low-key corporate leader rather than a larger-than-life public personality.

m9.evidence: He shifted Cisco toward recurring revenue and delivered record FY2026 revenue of $63.3B (up 11.8%) and net income of $13.3B, but revenue grew only from $49.8B in FY2021 and fell in FY2024.

m10.evidence: Cisco runs disciplined cost programs and restructurings, but it is not known for a distinctive culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: Cisco gear carries a large share of global internet, enterprise and government traffic, so its products indirectly underpin communication for billions of people.

p2.evidence: Designing high-speed routing silicon (Silicon One), carrier-grade operating systems and secure networks at global scale is very hard and is critical infrastructure for the internet and AI.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years (FY2021 $49.8B to FY2026 $63.3B) but fell 5.6% in FY2024 to $53.8B from $57.0B.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin was about flat (64.0% in FY2021 vs 64.5% in FY2026) and GAAP operating margin slipped from 25.8% to 24.3%.

f3.evidence: At July 25, 2026 debt was $29.5B versus $15.9B of cash and investments and $14.2B of FY2026 operating cash flow, with $50.3B of positive equity; leverage rose after the Splunk deal but is manageable.

f4.evidence: GAAP operating income rose from $12.8B in FY2021 to $15.4B in FY2026, but operating cash flow fell from $15.5B to $14.2B.

v1.evidence: Cisco is the broadest and most trusted enterprise option, but it is not clearly best in each category: Arista is often preferred in cloud data centers and Palo Alto/Fortinet in firewalls.

v2.evidence: Cisco ranked No. 3 on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For in 2026 and has repeatedly topped Great Place to Work's World's Best Workplaces list.

c5.evidence: If Cisco vanished, IT departments, telecom carriers and governments would struggle to run and secure their networks for years, though consumers would notice only indirectly and rivals could eventually replace it.
